title: Shankara and the man on the path
hookLine: a well-known scholar tells a man to get out of his way, and the man answers with a question about the Self
carry: jnana is knowing the one self in everyone

cards: Kashi, early morning. A young teacher, already well-known for his learning, is walking up from his bath in the Ganga with his students.

Coming toward him down the narrow lane is a man of the lowest caste, the kind the society of the day called untouchable, with four dogs at his heels. The teacher does what custom told him to do. Move aside, he says.
Get out of the way. The man doesn't move. He asks a question.

teach.h: 'BODY FROM BODY, OR SELF FROM SELF?'
teach.b: The teacher, tradition says, was Shankara, the great teacher of Advaita, non-duality. And the man's question, as the story is told: what do you want moved away? This body made of food, from that body made of food?
Or awareness from awareness? Is the sun any different, reflected in the Ganga or in a puddle in a poor man's lane?
Shankara stops. He has taught exactly this: that the one Self, Brahman, is the same in every being. Now a man in the street has shown him that he knew it only as an idea.

He bows, and a short poem credited to him says: whoever sees this way, whether outcaste or high-born, is my teacher. Many tellings add that the man was Shiva himself, and the four dogs the four Vedas. That's jnana.
Not knowing about, the way you can know the capital of a country you've never seen. Knowing directly, the way you know you're awake.
The book we open this week, the Vivekachudamani, the crest-jewel of discernment, also credited to Shankara, warns about this right away.
A flood of words and skill in explaining scripture give the learned a kind of enjoyment, it says, but they don't set anyone free.
Without realizing the oneness of the Self, there is no freedom. So on this teaching, you can't tell real jnana by what someone can recite. You can tell it by how they treat the person in the lane.

how: Some students of Advaita Vedanta read the Vivekachudamani slowly with a teacher, a few verses at a time, alongside periods of quiet reflection on what the verses point to.

o: skill in explaining the scriptures to others
a store of facts gathered from many books
direct, first-hand knowing, not just knowing about

games.q: the man on the path — tap the pairs.
p: asked: body from body, or Self from Self?
enjoyment for the learned, not freedom

s: the Vivekachudamani says learning scripture is the same as being free
it says skill in explaining scripture gives the learned enjoyment, but doesn't set anyone free.
Shankara bowed to the man he'd told to move aside
the man saw the one Self more truly than Shankara's own talk of it, and the poem credited to Shankara calls such a person his teacher.

games.q: you're Shankara. you just told a man to get out of your way, and he asks: move which, body from body, or Self from Self? what now?
o: bow: he knows what you only taught.
games.why: Shankara bowed, and the poem credited to him says whoever sees the one Self, low-born or priest, is his teacher. that's jnana: knowing, not knowing about.

practice: Bring to mind one person you'll pass today without really seeing: the one who cleans, the driver, the auntie stacking chairs after the program.

For a few breaths, set down the labels, the job, the clothes, the place in line, and rest on the plain fact that they're aware, just as you are. That shared awareness is what Shankara's teaching calls the one Self.
If you pray, bow inwardly to the Lord in them, as Shankara bowed in the lane; if not, simply notice how the labels loosen.

wordCard.voice: Jnana. Knowing, the direct kind, not knowing about. In Shankara's story it's the knowing that sees one Self in the man in the lane, which no amount of clever talk can stand in for.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: jnana, knowing. Often spoken as gyaan in Hindi.

carryVoice: Your line: jnana is knowing the one self in everyone. Not borrowed, but seen. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Manisha Panchakam (credited to Shankara), verse 1 and refrain ('chandalo 'stu sa tu dvijo 'stu gurur ity esha manisha mama'); the Kashi meeting as told in the traditional lives of Shankara
